extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, ombudsmen, and journalism students interested in ethics and newsroom accountability
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for newsroom verification, use of unnamed sources, corrections, and the ombudsman role illustrated by the Janet Cooke/Jimmy’s World case. Focuses on how editors and ombudsmen should detect, investigate, and publicly address journalistic fabrication and systemic editorial failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reporters to reveal source identity to editors or withhold publication
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the reporter can’t support the integrity of his or her story by revealing the name to his or her editor, the story shouldn’t be published. And if that safeguard prevents some news stories from appearing, so be it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a strict safeguarding standard: anonymous sourcing that cannot be validated to an editor is grounds to block publication. The Cooke case illustrates the risk when editors never required confidential identification of 'Jimmy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Default toward naming sources; restrict unnamed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: “Naming names is the standard, or should be.” Also noted: the New York Times adopted new standards against the use of unnamed sources because in rare cases stories using this device proved false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat unnamed sources as exceptional; require strong justification and additional verification when anonymity is used. The page cites organizational policy changes (e.g., NYT) as precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge mistakes and correct them promptly and prominently
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted from the Society of Professional Journalists ethics code: “Acknowledge mistakes and correct them promptly and prominently.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When errors or fabrication are discovered, publish clear corrections/apologies and make them prominent to rebuild credibility. The Post issued an editorial apology and the Pulizer was returned, illustrating remedial actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose unethical conduct within the organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Also from SPJ ethics code: journalists should “expose unethical conduct in journalism, including within their organizations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations and ombudsmen should investigate and publicize internal ethical breaches rather than conceal them. Green’s detailed public report is offered as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify facts rigorously — 'If your mother says she loves you, check it out.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification imperative captured by the aphorism: “If your mother says she loves you, check it out.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat all claims skeptically and verify independently. The Cooke story failed because editors did not sufficiently check reported facts and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reporters' biographical claims and credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should confirm background claims (e.g., Cooke’s false claims about degrees were discovered by calls to colleges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform routine checks of journalists’ résumés and biographical assertions, especially before elevating or awarding high-profile pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require and examine contemporaneous notes and recordings as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post’s editors examined Cooke’s notes and listened to recorded interviews and found there were no notes or tapes about Jimmy and his family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should retain and editors should review contemporaneous notes, recordings, and documentation that substantiate reporting. Lack of such materials is a serious red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors and supervisors must actively demand source identification and exercise oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical failure noted: “Not a single Post supervisor had asked Cooke to identify Jimmy, even confidentially.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisors should proactively question reporters about how sources were found and demand verification, not defer unquestioningly to a reporter’s account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let a drive for impact override basic verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Green criticised a newsroom where “a drive for impact overrode several experienced journalists’ doubts that Jimmy actually existed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize accuracy and verification over sensationalism or expediency. Editorial ambition is not a substitute for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ombudsman should be independent, fearless, thorough, even-handed, and propose fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Green’s work is described as the gold standard: a no-holds-barred, meticulously reported account that “pulls no punches and offers recommendations to fix the problems.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An in-house reader advocate/ombudsman should conduct transparent investigations, be willing to criticize the organization publicly, report even-handedly, and provide concrete recommendations to prevent future failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescind honors and awards when fraud is uncovered
rubrics_metrics.description: When fabrication was confirmed, the Pulitzer board withdrew Cooke’s prize and gave it to the runner-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations should correct institutional recognition (e.g., revoke awards) when reporting is proven fraudulent, as part of restoring integrity and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication and deception are unacceptable and disqualify reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooke’s article was a fabrication and she later stated: the article “was a serious misrepresentation which I deeply regret.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication is a fundamental breach of journalistic ethics; stories found to be fabricated require resignation, retractions, corrections, and institutional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct transparent, public investigations and publish findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Green wrote an 18,000‑word public report detailing what went wrong — described as a model of ombudsmanship for confronting flaws and admitting them publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough public reports documenting failures, methods, interviews, and recommendations help restore public trust and serve as instructional cases for the profession.
